cells.tense: You're here, present, and the connection is actually landing right now.
cells.ask: Offer one feeling you've been holding back, and let whatever comes back sit there without fixing it.
cells.core:
You walk into a room and something starts moving. Not by force — by the fact that you actually want to be there, and you don't hide it. You ask the real question, tell the honest story, let the room feel like it matters. And because you stay close to what people are feeling rather than above it, they come with you. That's not a trick. That's the thing itself.
What keeps it steady is you know the difference between real connection and a performance of it. You check yourself — is this mine to say? — and the checking is quiet and quick. So the energy goes somewhere instead of scattering. Watch for the moment you start steering instead of feeling, though. The pull to make it happen is the same current that made it real, and it doesn't take much for steering to take over.
cells.sheetLine: You bring the feeling, and the feeling brings people.
cells.verb: charging into what connects, and making others feel it too
cells.place: beside someone, feeling what they're feeling, and staying

cells.tense: You're already in the next room, rehearsing what that connection will feel like, before anyone has spoken here.
cells.ask: Stop mid-push and name one thing the other person actually said, in their own words, before you say another word of yours.
cells.core:
You're pushing the connection to happen ahead of time. Before anyone's ready, before the moment's earned it, you're already arranging how it should go — the right question, the right opening, the right feeling to give them. You can feel the pull to make it land now, because you know it could, and waiting feels like a waste.
But that pushing doesn't speed anything up. It puts your idea of the connection where the real one should be. The other person can feel the gap even if they can't name it. What would help is letting the structure break when it needs to. Say the thing once, then stop. Let the silence do its part. You don't have to be the one who makes it move every second.

cells.tense: You were in that conversation once, and some part of you never actually left it.
cells.ask: Write three sentences about one thing you understand about how someone works, then say it to them.
cells.core:
There's a distance between you and the people around you now. Not coldness — you care, and you can feel it when someone's hurting or needing something. But you've stopped moving toward them. You watch the connection happen, or you remember how it used to feel, and you don't step in. The pull toward real contact is still there. You're just standing back from it.
That's because the part of you that makes meaning — that sees the pattern and says the true thing — has gone quiet. Not gone. Quiet. If you start there, with the understanding instead of the feeling, it comes back. Explain one thing you've noticed about someone. Put it into words. The feeling follows the explaining, not the other way around.

cells.tense: You're already shaping how this group makes meaning together, and you keep calling it just how things go.
cells.ask: Claim one thing you've already shaped — a habit, a ritual, the way a room talks — and say out loud that you made it that way.
cells.core:
Something happens in the rooms you're in, and it's not random. People echo your phrasing back. The way you ask a question sets the tone others follow. A small ritual you started has become just what happens now. You're doing that. You did it on purpose, even if you've never said so.
The part that's missing isn't the shaping. You're already there. What's missing is saying so. You keep calling it just how things are here when you're the one who made it that way. Naming it won't make it heavy or fake — it'll just mean you know what you're doing. And when you know, you can choose it instead of just watching it run.
